verdict.rationale: Auth0's docs show it acting as an OAuth 2.0 authorization server for your own API. It issues access tokens to applications that authenticate with a Client ID and Secret, and it supports scopes and permissions for third-party integrations, which covers the core of being a token issuer for outside clients. The evidence is thin on the end-to-end "Sign in with my app" experience for third-party developers. Missing for 10: documentation of third-party client registration or onboarding, consent screens for third-party apps, branding the provider under your own app identity, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can turn my own application into an OAuth provider that issues tokens to third-party clients ("Sign in with my app")

citations.quote: You built an API and you want to secure it with OAuth 2.0.
Handle authorization using scopes and granular permissions, whether it's for first-party apps, third-party integrations, or Machine-to-Machine communications.
Applications authenticate themselves to Auth0 via their Client Id and Client Secret. Auth0 verifies the information and responds with an Access Token.
